@graph.headline: Who Measures the Ocean's Plastic? GDP and the Global Microplastics Data Gap
@graph.description: Wealth predicts which countries get their waters tested for microplastics: GDP vs 29,076 NOAA records, and the map gaps that result.
@graph.keywords: microplastics, ocean, data, justice, R, environmental, monitoring

mainEntity.name: Does a country's GDP really predict how much its waters get tested for microplastics?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, moderately and significantly in this database: Spearman rho = 0.33 between GDP and record count (p = 0.007, n = 66 countries), rising to rho = 0.36 for records per million people against GDP per capita. It is a rank correlation over observational data, so it shows association, not proof of mechanism.

mainEntity.name: Why is the equator a gap if that's where shipping and fishing concentrate?

acceptedAnswer.text: Because the database records where researchers sample, not where plastic is. Sampling clusters around funded institutions in temperate northern countries; the equatorial dip (786 records between 0 and 10 degrees North) reflects research geography, not pollution geography.

mainEntity.name: What dataset can I use to do this correlation myself?

acceptedAnswer.text: NOAA NCEI's harmonized marine microplastics database (a single CSV, 1972-present) for testing effort, joined on its country field, and the World Bank's GDP indicator (NY.GDP.MKTP.CD) via its free API for wealth. The post's mp_gdp_correlation.R script does the full join and correlation.

mainEntity.name: What are the limitations of this analysis?

acceptedAnswer.text: Three: the country field covers 40.2% of records and marks sampling location rather than funder; the database harmonizes heterogeneous methods, so record counts measure effort, not comparable pollution levels; and the US contributes 78% of country-tagged records, though the correlation holds without it.
